newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Singapore government plays cupid.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Singapore government plays cupid.

text.p: Love and marriage are such serious subjects to the Singapore government that it often doesn't leave them to chance.
The Social Development Unit (SDU) serves as a sort of matchmaker and dating service for single, professional Singaporeans trying to find a life-long mate.
It caters to university graduates, while another government agency plays Cupid to those who fail to get to a university.
The National University Hospital recently gave its single employees five days paid leave to attend an SDU-organised event in the hope of finding a spouse.
"Most of the people who are above 30 just don't have the time," said Tina Quake, an SDU member who works as a financial controller for a U.S. company in Singapore.
"It's difficult to find somebody because the expectations are so high," she told Reuters in an interview.
The SDU has thrived, apparently because of official concern over Singapore's falling reproduction rate and the seeming reluctance of professionals to get married.

The city-state's Straits Times newspaper, citing a study by the National University of Singapore and the Institute of Policy Studies, said last year that the country's women, on average, had 1.8 children.
A reproduction rate of just over 2.1 percent annually is considered necessary to maintain a stable population in most countries.
STIGMA LINGERS OVER SDU MEMBERSHIP
But the SDU is still the butt of jokes among the young, who say it stands for "Single, desperate and ugly".
One SDU member said it was formed because the children of some government officials could not find partners.

"There's a stigma about joining it," said one Singaporean woman, who did not want to be named. Membership seems to brand the person as someone who does not have the ability to begin and sustain a relationship, she said.
The SDU declined a written request for an interview, saying officials were "too busy." There are an estimated 19,000 people on its membership rolls.
Many of the Singaporeans joining up no longer think of finding somebody to marry, however.
"The young people use this to socialise," Quake said. "Most of the members today are very young."
She said the SDU is now useful for networking to push one's career along.
GROUP BOWLING AND DANCING COURSES
Activities organised by the SDU range from group bowling dates to ballroom dancing. There's even a course to instruct Singaporeans on using the correct glass for a particular wine.

There are courses on tennis, badminton, mountain climbing and swimming. The SDU also offered a trip with 40 other Singaporeans to the Indonesian resort island of Batam. Another excursion took romance-seekers all the way to Nepal.
For the painfully shy there is Tele-pal, an electronic matching service first started by Singapore's Ministry of Defence, which was concerned about the large number of single officers in its ranks.
The SDU said at the time the service was launched that Tele-pal could be a substitute for a direct meeting.
"It opens doors, but members must follow through with a personal meeting," the SDU said.
PRESSURE TO MARRY UNCOMFORTABLY STRONG
The pressure to settle down and have children in a conservative society like Singapore remains very strong, and at times, uncomfortably so.
"The older folks, they press the younger folks to settle down," Quake said.
In a television special on three Singaporeans using the SDU to find partners, parents and relatives of the trio kept pestering them with questions on when they were going to get married.
"It makes me want to get married," said a local radio station employee named Madeleine.
The situation is complicated by the fact that more women in Singapore are getting an education, which may intimidate some suitors.
"To a certain degree, they're intimidated," Quake said. "They're afraid. The girls don't marry down. The men don't marry up."
